These results validate parametrized IQP circuits as a practical tool for generative modeling on near-term devices, while clearly delineating the critical challenges that must be addressed for future progress.
237: Quantum computing continues to face challenges in scaling both qubit quality and quantity, motivating the shift toward Distributed Quantum Computing (DQC), where multiple interconnected Quantum Processing Units (QPUs) collaboratively solve problems too complex for monolithic systems. In a quantum data center, QPUs distributed across racks can perform remote gate operations by creating entanglement between them, enabling circuit execution through DQC. However, generating end-to-end entangled pairs in a quantum data center often causes congestion and resource contention. To mitigate this, we introduce a resource management framework with efficient schedulers that maximize fidelity-guaranteed throughput while preserving the dependency constraints of sub-circuits derived from the original quantum circuit. We benchmark the scheduling problem using a MixedInteger Linear Programming (MILP) model and then propose a set of lightweight schedulers-Least Resource First (LRF) and its extension, Group LRF (GLRF). These lightweight schedulers provide practical, though less optimal, solutions for handling the high volume of remote gates in DQC workloads. Our initial results on a DCell-based quantum data center show that such heuristics perform well under current DQC conditions, balancing runtime and performance while avoiding the heavy overhead of solvers or machine learning approaches, which often struggle to meet the strict timing demands of short-lived entanglement.
238: Quantum error correction is critical for protecting quantum computations from noise, yet standard protocols demand significant qubit overhead. To address this, we introduce a learning-based approach that allows tailoring encodings to specific noise channels. This approach is based on a novel loss function that maximizes the distinguishability of noisy quantum states. We thereby realize a variational quantum algorithm that discovers new resource-efficient codes, which empirically outperform standard quantum error correction schemes on various noise structures. We furthermore derive promising theoretical properties of these variational quantum error correction (VarQEC) codes and perform proof-of-concept experiments on quantum hardware.
239: We present a framework for implementing two-qubit entangling operations between distant superconducting qubits using a space-time modulated Josephson junction (JJ) metasurface. By modulating the surface in both space and time, we engineer sidebands with controllable wavevectors that selectively couple target qubits. The metasurface acts as a reconfigurable coupling medium, where the interaction strength is determined by engineered transmission coefficients $T_{\mu}\left(\mathrm{k}_{\mu} \cdot \mathrm{r}\right)$ rather than by exponentially decaying near-field coupling, thus reducing the dependence on physical proximity. We investigated the implementation of two-qubit interactions via iSWAP gates driven resonantly through the metasurface and controlled phase gates via geometric phase accumulation. Simulations show entangling fidelity exceeding 98% maintained over centimeter-scale separations.
240: This paper proposes a dataflow-based optimization method called Quantum Intermediate Representation Optimization (QIRopt) within the LLVM infrastructure. QIRopt has two main functions: preprocessing QIR code to expose more optimization opportunities to the LLVM optimizer and optimizing QIR code to avoid redundant loading and construction of qubits and qubit arrays. We evaluated QIRopt on the IBM Challenge Dataset, and the results demonstrate its effectiveness in reducing redundant operations in QIR code. A preliminary implementation of QIRopt and a case study on real-world code further confirm that our approach enhances the LLVM optimizer's ability to optimize preprocessed QIR code.
241: We present a method for constructing shallow quantum circuits to simulate molecular vibrations on near-term quantum devices. Derived from Givens rotation unitaries, we achieved more than 50 % reduction in the circuit depth compared to the unitary vibrational coupled cluster approach.
242: Parrondo's paradox shows that alternating two losing strategies can yield a net positive outcome—a counterintuitive effect relevant to probabilistic systems and control. We demonstrate a quantum analogue using single-qubit inhomogeneous quantum walk—unlike prior work that required multi-coin or position-dependent constructions. Instead, we apply a local phase gate at the origin and alternate two fixed $\text{SU}(2)$ coins, with parameters from recent inhomogeneous quantum walks. Sequence ABB yields positive displacement despite no individual bias. This establishes that coherent interference alone can reproduce the Parrondo effect in single-qubit systems, with implications for low-cost quantum algorithms and transport protocols.
243: Continuous variable (CV) measurement-deviceindependent (MDI) quantum key distribution (QKD) offers a more robust method to achieve unconditionally secure communications relative to standard CV-QKD. Here, we propose a novel implementation of CV-MDI-QKD that is tolerant to noise and channel loss across a broad range of operational conditions, where a fraction of the optical reference pulses, normally used for local local oscillator construction, is sacrificed for classical communication throughput. We demonstrate that our new protocol enables seamless inclusion of optical classical communication in satellite channels at surprisingly with minimal compromise to the quantum communication performance. Simulation results show that the cost of classical-quantum multiplexing to the QKD key rate as a function of the parameters in many settings is almost negligible. This trade-off implies that high-bandwidth classical communication can be achieved for “almost-free,” and further opens a scalable path for enhancements in the emerging quantum internet.
244: In this paper, we propose a Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) formulation for solving the classical $k$-Nearest Neighbors ($k$-NN) problem and demonstrate its efficacy. We use a quantum annealer for solving the QUBO. We tested the model on a dataset containing 1,000 text documents. Our model was able to predict the “class” of a test document accurately. Our findings highlight the promise of QUBO-based methods for scalable, hybrid quantum-classical machine learning.
245: Random number generation (RNG) is necessary for secure and random quantum computing operations. This paper proposes and compares two quantum RNG methods: pseudo-random and quasi-random. Hadamard gates are used by the quasi-random method, which is well-suited for errortolerant quantum systems. We compare the two methods with IBM Qiskit using various qubit sizes by running each setup 1,000 times. Critical performance measures such as total simulation time, mean runtime, chi-square value, p-value, and Shannon entropy are quantified to compare efficiency and randomness quality. Quasirandom methods yield higher entropy and more evenly distributed values, especially with larger numbers of qubits. Pseudo-random methods are nevertheless computationally more cost-effective and yield more stable statistical outcomes, which qualify them best for applications where speed is critical. These findings illustrate a quality of randomness versus computational efficiency trade-off that offers insight to selecting the proper RNG technique based on application needs in quantum systems.
246: Variational quantum algorithms, which use a classical computer to optimize parameters of a quantum circuit, have emerged as a promising solution for near-term quantum computing due to their inherent resilience to the noise and computational inaccuracies of current quantum devices. However, current quantum compilers overlook the approximate nature of these quantum circuits. We present Bifrost, a new transpilation methodology designed specifically for variational quantum algorithms that introduces a novel form of approximate compilation. This produces more hardware-efficient and noise-robust quantum circuits for variational quantum algorithms while maintaining high accuracy. Our experimental results demonstrate that Bifrost can leverage approximate compilation techniques to maintain similar theoretical level of accuracy on quantum application benchmarks while reducing CNOT gate count by up to 38%. In practice, Bifrost transpilation results in both 10 – 17% faster execution and 9 – 23% error reduction on real quantum hardware. We further find that approximately compiled ansatze can be used to guide the design of larger ansatze and that the Bifrost methodology can adapt to improvements in quantum hardware.
247: We consider multi-qubit entangled quantum states known in the literature as one-layer variational quantum states. The states can also be considered as quantum graph states representing directed and weighted graphs. The corresponding variational quantum protocols include $R Y, R Z$, and entangling blocks with $R X X$ gates. We examine the general case in which the entangling blocks have an arbitrary structure, namely, $R X X$ gates are applied to arbitrary pairs of qubits. This case corresponds to an arbitrary structure of the associated weighted and directed graphs. Variational quantum states, as well as quantum graph states, have broad applications in various fields of quantum computing, including quantum machine learning, quantum error correction, and optimization algorithms, and others. One of the key resources in quantum computing is entanglement. We analytically calculate the entanglement distance for variational quantum states with entangling blocks of arbitrary structure. The dependence of entanglement on the parameters of the variational quantum state and on the characteristics of the corresponding weighted and directed graphs is investigated. We find that the entanglement of a qubit with other qubits in the state depends on the outdegree and indegree of the corresponding vertex in the graph, as well as on the weights of the incoming and outgoing arcs associated with that vertex. Quantum protocols for quantifying the entanglement distance of variational quantum states have been constructed. For particular cases of variational quantum states, the dependence of entanglement distance on the state parameters has been examined using quantum computation on the Aer simulator.
248: We investigate the absolute calibration of single photon detectors (SPDs) based on a portable bi-photon source. We study the impact of multi-photon quantum states from the source on the calibration accuracy and develop a theoretical model to account for this and other effects. Our work provides a path towards practical absolute SPD calibration for future standardized photonic quantum technologies.
249: We are currently working on a platform for preparing spin-squeezed states in a large atomic ensemble through quantum measurement backaction. Our approach involves using the birefringence interaction of a light probe with an atomic ensemble that is prepared in a superposition of the clock states within the ground state manifold of cesium atoms. To enhance the atom-light interaction and increase the fidelity of state preparation, we will utilize a high optical depth (OD) ensemble along with shot noise-limited polarimetry. We are currently working on increasing the OD by increasing the optical power for laser cooling and trapping by introducing a tapered amplifier into the setup. We expect that this platform will enable efficient generation of spin squeezing in a large atomic ensemble.
250: The design and implementation of quantum circuits is becoming increasingly challenging due to the technological limitations of quantum computers. To overcome these hurdles, distributed quantum computation has proved useful, making quantum processors cooperate. However, currently available circuit distribution methods focus on unitary operations, while a quantum computer, in order to be capable of performing any general task, must be able to perform a larger class of operations, described by completely positive maps. This work proposes a novel workflow for circuit distribution algorithms addressing this gap, contributing to progress toward fully capable quantum computation.
251: Current superconducting quantum computing architectures are designed in such a way that each qubit is locally controlled with a dedicated drive and, sometimes, flux line. Scaling up these architectures to larger chips sizes and qubit counts is problematic, as the increased number of wires in the system would produce additional crosstalk and thermal load, as well as increasing costs. Recently, there have been a number of proposals to overcome this wiring bottleneck. These proposals rely on engineering a large $\mathbf{Z Z}$ interaction between neighboring qubits in order to enter the so-called blockade regime, which enables the execution of logical operations with only three global drive lines regardless of the number of qubits on the chip. In these architectures, the entire dynamics is governed by the ZZ interaction, which needs to be the dominant energy scale to preserve the blockade regime. We present here preliminary results showing the possibility of retaining a large $\mathbf{Z Z}$ coupling between two strongly detuned qubits, with an increase of several orders of magnitude with respect to what has been reported so far in the literature. In particular, we measure the $\mathbf{Z Z}$ coupling between two capacitively-coupled transmon qubits and extract a ZZ strength of 22 MHz for a detuning of 2.4 GHz, placing our system well into the blockade regime. These findings provide an experimental validation of the working principle of several global quantum computing architectures and represent a first step towards their practical realization.
252: Grover's algorithm is one of the most significant quantum algorithms, enabling the search for a marked element in an unsorted database quadratically faster than classical search algorithms. We utilize Groves's algorithm to detect the edges of a digital image faster than any classical edge detection methods. The high success probability of our method in detecting image edges, compared to most existing quantum edge detection methods, makes it a more suitable candidate for use in the presence of noise on current quantum devices. We implemented our model for the $2 \times 2$ blocks of the image using a two-qubit Qiskit circuit with the QASM simulator and the noisy IBM Sydney(fake) device, making it suitable for most of the current NISQ devices.
253: State-of-the-art quantum circuit optimization (QCO) algorithms for T-count reduction often lead to a substantial increase in two-qubit gate count (2Q-count)-a drawback that existing 2Q-count optimization techniques struggle to address effectively. In this work, we propose a novel lazy resynthesis approach for modern tableau-based QCO flows that significantly mitigates the 2 Q -gate surges commonly introduced during T-count optimization in Clifford+T circuits. Experimental results show that our approach reduces 2 Q-count overhead by $54.8 \%, 15.3 \%$, and $\mathbf{6 8. 0} \%$ compared to tableau-based, ZX-calculus-based, and path-sum-based QCO algorithms, respectively. In terms of runtime, our method achieves speedups of $1.81 \times$ and $13.1 \times$ over the tableau-based and ZX-calculus-based methods, while performing comparably to the path-sum-based approach. In summary, the proposed lazy resynthesis technique not only enhances the quality and performance of tableau-based QCO algorithms but also demonstrates superior efficiency and scalability compared to alternative QCO approaches such as ZX-calculus and path-sumbased techniques.
254: The surface code family is a promising approach to implementing fault-tolerant quantum computations. Universal fault-tolerance quantum computing requires error-corrected nonClifford operations, in addition to Clifford gates, and for the former, it is important to experimentally demonstrate additional resources known as magic states. Another challenge is to efficiently embed surface codes into quantum hardware with connectivity constraints. This work simultaneously addresses both challenges by employing a qubit-efficient rotated heavyhexagonal surface code for IBM quantum processors (ibm_fez) and implementing the magic state injection protocol. Our work reports error thresholds for both logical bit- and phase-flip errors, of $\approx 0.37 \%$ and $\approx 0.31 \%$, respectively, which are higher than the threshold values previously reported with traditional embedding. The post-selection-based preparation of logical magic states $\vert H_{L}\rangle$ and $\vert T_{L}\rangle$ achieves fidelities of $0.8806 \pm 0.0002$ and $0.8665 \pm 0.0003$, respectively, which are both above the magic state distillation threshold. Our work demonstrates the potential for realising nonClifford logical gates by producing high-fidelity logical magic states on IBM quantum devices.
255: Recent advances in quantum linear solvers offer a promising direction for accelerating extreme scientific computations such as fluid dynamics. However, the deep and complex circuits required by many quantum algorithms limit their practical use on current quantum hardware. The Variational Quantum Linear Solver (VQLS) presents a viable alternative for near-term quantum devices (NISQ), and initial efforts have explored its application to select fluid dynamics problems. In this work, we evaluate the use of VQLS for canonical fluid dynamics problems, aiming to identify pathways for generalizing its implementation across a broader class of systems. We analyze the impact of various circuit ansatz and classical optimizers on solution quality and convergence behavior. Furthermore, we assess the algorithm's feasibility within a hybrid quantum–high-performance computing (HPC) framework by porting it to QFw, a state-of-the-art quantum-HPC software stack. 11This manuscript has been authored by UT-Battelle, LLC, under contract DE-AC05-00OR22725 with the US Department of Energy (DOE). 256: Ising machines can efficiently solve combinatorial optimization problems by mapping them to Ising or QUBO formulations while satisfying given constraints. However, their hardware limits the size of QUBO instances. To overcome this, subQUBO annealing decomposes large problems into smaller ones. Meanwhile, conventional subQUBO construction methods often violate the constraints originally given. In this paper, we propose a grid reduction method for subQUBO construction that explicitly considers the 2-way 1-hot constraint. It recursively fixes a variable to 1 and sets all other variables in the same row and column to 0. Remaining variables are used to construct subQUBOs with three strategies: index-based, deviation-based, and random-based extraction. Evaluation experiments using a real Ising machine demonstrates significant energy reduction over existing subQUBO construction methods.
257: To address the qubit overhead of encoding objective function values on Grover adaptive search, we propose a qubit-width-aware algorithm that reduces the number of qubits by scaling the dynamic range, without compromising solution quality. Specifically, we analyze the trade-off between accuracy and performance under hardware constraints. Simulations on the Personalized Course Selection Problem (PCSP), a realistic scheduling task with preferences and constraints, demonstrate that our method reduces qubit usage by up to 7 qubits while maintaining the original success rate.
258: Large-scale fault-tolerant quantum computation requires compiling logical circuits into physical operations tailored to a given architecture. Prior work addressing this challenge has mostly focused on the surface code and lattice surgery schemes. In this work, we broaden the scope by considering lattice surgery compilation for topological codes beyond the surface code. We begin by defining a code substrate-a blueprint for implementing topological codes and lattice surgery. We then abstract from the microscopic details and rephrase the compilation task as a mapping and routing problem on a macroscopic routing graph, potentially subject to substrate-specific constraints. We explore specific substrates and codes, including the color code and the folded surface code, providing detailed microscopic constructions. For the color code, we present numerical simulations analyzing how design choices at the microscopic and macroscopic levels affect the depth of compiled logical CNOT + T circuits. An opensource code is available on GitHub https://github.com/cda-tum/mqt-qecc.
259: Efficient and adaptive placement of virtualized RAN functions is crucial to satisfy the diverse and dynamic Quality of Service (QoS) requirements in 5G networks. While blackbox optimization methods such as Factorization Machine with Annealing (FMA) have shown promise for combinatorial optimization problems with limited data, their adaptability is limited in dynamic environments due to their reliance on historical data. In this paper, we propose an enhanced FMA approach that incorporates a Transformer-based time-series prediction model to calibrate the surrogate parameters at each time step, enabling adaptation to dynamic environments. Numerical experiments in simulated RAN environments demonstrate that the proposed calibration achieves a 0.50% improvement in mean QoS satisfaction ratio over that of standard FMA when a moderate calibration coefficient is used, providing the best tradeoff between adaptability and robustness.
260: With the increasing emphasis on energy efficiency and sustainability, optimizing the energy supply of base stations, the major energy consumers in communication networks, has become a critical problem. In addition, for real-time and scalable energy optimization in sustainable base station systems, it is necessary to obtain highly-efficient solutions in a shorter time. We formulate the base station power optimization problem as a Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) problem, where the goal is to minimize a combination of power costs while satisfying operational constraints. Furthermore, to improve computational efficiency, we propose a QUBO simplification method that cuts down QUBO coefficients with small absolute values to zero. We solve both the original and simplified QUBOs using an Ising machine. Experimental results show that our QUBO simplification approach accelerates computation by up to 10 X on large-scale instances, with minimal degradation in solution quality.
261: We introduce a set of quantum ansätze tailored for computing Green's functions of single-impurity models using the variational quantum eigensolver. These ansätze conserve particle number and spin, allowing for the efficient preparation of the impurity model's ground state and the Krylov bases required to express the Green's function as a continued fraction. Notably, the parameters preparing the particle and hole excitations used as initial Krylov vectors are fully determined by those optimized for the ground state, eliminating the need for secondary optimizations or alternative excitation preparation methods. We demonstrate the utility of these ansätze by computing Green's functions for single-impurity Anderson models with one bath site within a dynamical mean-field theory loop, where the impuritybath hybridization is updated self-consistently. The parameters defining the states in the Krylov bases are straightforwardly determined by orthonormality in the single-bath case, allowing for the direct computation of the relevant Hamiltonian matrix elements from these states. Future work will explore the robustness, scalability, and practical integration of these ansätze into hybrid quantum-classical simulations of strongly correlated materials.
262: Ising machines, including quantum annealing machines, are promising for solving combinatorial optimization problems with high quality solutions. For constrained combinatorial optimization problems, choosing appropriate penalty coefficients is crucial for obtaining better feasible solutions. When tackling the large-scale combinatorial optimization problems, the variable reduction method is one of the most effective methods. To address these difficulties, we propose a new variable reduction method called multi-penalty sample persistence variable reduction (MP-SPVAR). The method is based on the sample persistence variable reduction method, and utilizes the solution samples across multiple penalty coefficients to fix the variables. The proposed method is evaluated on the 60-facility quadratic assignment problem tai60b from QAPLIB using an Ising machine. The experimental results show that MP-SPVAR can obtain better feasible solutions than solving the problem without any variable reduction. The proposed method is promising for solving the large-scale constrained combinatorial optimization problems with Ising machines.
263: Ising machines, including quantum annealing machines, are promising next-generation computers for combinatorial optimization problems. Due to hardware limitations, most Ising-type hardware can only solve functions expressed in linear or quadratic terms of binary variables. Therefore, problems with higher-order terms require order reduction, which increases the number of variables and constraints and may degrade solution quality. This study evaluates the effectiveness of directly solving such problems without order reduction by using the polynomial unconstrained binary optimization (PUBO) solver implemented in Toshiba's Simulated Quantum-inspired Bifurcation Machine+ (SQBM+). We compare its performance against a conventional quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) solver on the same hardware platform. As benchmarks, we use a vehicle routing problem with distance balancing and the low autocorrelation binary sequence (LABS) problem, both of which naturally include higher-order interactions. Results show that the PUBO solver consistently achieves superior solution quality and stability compared to its QUBO counterpart, while maintaining comparable computational time and requiring no order-reduction compilation, indicating the potential advantages of directly handling higher-order terms in practical optimization problems.
264: As quantum computation continues to advance, distributed quantum computing is emerging as a crucial configuration, offering a means to leverage the best technology across diverse platforms. This approach is essential for enhancing scalability and advancing quantum resources towards faulttolerant demonstration. A fundamental element of this design is the establishment of scalable quantum networks with robust quantum memory systems. We have recently demonstrated a high efficiency and high bandwidth solid-state quantum memory developed for the Quantum-Accelerated Internet Testbed (QuAInT) at Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL), reaching $28.5 \pm 0.2 \%$ efficiency and a 630 MHz absorption window in the material. This work for QuAInT represents a collaborative endeavor across multiple institutions to establish the groundwork for a national quantum internet connection. We will highlight that work here, as well as our strategic vision to build a lower temperature and low-latency quantum memory platform.
265: Machine Learning with deep neural networks has transformed computational approaches to scientific and engineering problems. Central to many of these advancements are precisely tuned neural architectures that are tailored to the domains in which they are used. In this work, we develop deep learning techniques and architectural modifications that improve performance on reinforcement learning guided quantum circuit synthesis-the task of constructing a circuit that implements a given unitary matrix. First, we propose a global phase invariance operation which makes our architecture resilient to complex global phase shifts. Second, we demonstrate how augmenting data with small random unitary perturbations during training enables more robust learning. Finally, we show how encoding numerical data with techniques from image processing allow networks to better detect small but significant changes in data. Our work enables deep learning approaches to better synthesize quantum circuits that implement unitary matrices.
266: We present a framework for developing quantum networks that enables a gradual transition from classical to fully quantum communication infrastructures. The proposed framework is based on the incorporation of a quantum overlay network on top of the classical network infrastructure, which can be incrementally expanded in alignment with technological advancements, market demand, and available investment. Central to this approach is the concept of an intermittent quantum IQ network, wherein only a subset of network links is quantum-secured, forming a spatially intermittent quantum network (sIQ network). Furthermore, the selection of such links can change over time, leading to the realization of a space-time intermittent quantum network (stIQ network), offering flexibility and scalability in the deployment of quantum communication technologies.
267: The localization of electron confinement states in InAs/GaAs double quantum dots (DQDs) is described by two-level system theory [1] and is known to depend on the material properties, size and shape of the quantum dots, and the presence of externally-applied fields [2]. We present results from three-dimensional (3D) computational models of electron localization in DQDs and show that the ideal coherence of the symmetrical DQDs can be destroyed by any small violation of physical symmetry, but can be rectified by applying a weak electric field. This has applications to quantum computing and biochemical sensors.
268: Protein folding is an NP-hard optimization problem that quantum algorithms may help solve more efficiently. The Quantum Metropolis Algorithm (QMA) provides a promising framework for simulating folding dynamics via quantum sampling, but its scalability on NISQ devices is limited by circuit depth and rigid annealing schedules. We propose a hybrid clas-sical-quantum framework that decomposes the folding process into shallow quantum walk steps and adaptively adjusts the inverse temperature parameter $\beta$ between iterations. Specifically, we introduce two annealing strategies: an adaptive method that leverages Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence and overlap with the target low-energy state, and a Bayesian method based on probabilistic modeling. Simulations on dipeptides, tripeptides, and tetrapeptides demonstrate that these methods match or surpass prior geometric schedules, achieving potential quantum advantage.
269: The computational demands of geoscientific workflows are rapidly increasing in both complexity and scale, pushing the limits of classical computing. Quantum computing has emerged as a promising paradigm to address some of these challenges. This paper surveys the growing intersection between quantum computing and energy geosciences, highlighting recent developments and initiatives. To illustrate the practical relevance of this emerging field, we present a case study on seismic traveltime inversion using a variational quantum circuit. In this example, a hybrid quantum-classical workflow is used to reconstruct velocity models from noisy traveltime data, demonstrating how quantum circuits can solve geophysical inverse problems. While modest in scale, the study offers insights into the formulation and implementation of quantumassisted inversion. As quantum hardware advances and algorithmic frameworks mature, quantum computing is poised to become a transformative tool in the computational landscape of energy geosciences.
270: When undertaking continuous-variable quantum key distribution (CV-QKD) across atmospheric channels, strong classical local oscillators (LOs) are often polarization-multiplexed with the weak quantum signals for coherent measurement at the receiver. Although the wavefronts of the quantum signal and LO are often assumed to experience the same distortion across channels, previous theoretical work has shown that they can experience differential distortions, resulting in relative wavefront errors (WFEs). Such errors have previously been shown to limit CV-QKD performance, in some cases leading to zero secure key rates. In this work, for the first time, we provide strong experimental evidence that relative WFEs are present in some circumstances and that standard assumptions in CVQKD deployments may need to be revisited. In addition, we demonstrate how turbulence can affect the detailed form of the relative WFEs, thereby indicating that long-range links like terrestrial-satellite channels are likely impacted more than shortrange terrestrial-only channels.
271: Quantum oracles are essential components in quantum algorithms, enabling the efficient evaluation of Boolean functions. This paper presents a novel approach to constructing resource-efficient data-lookup quantum oracles for fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) systems. By leveraging the algebraic normal form (ANF) of Boolean functions, rather than the truth tables used in existing approaches, we achieve a provable $\mathcal{O}(n)$ reduction in the minimum Toffoli gate count - a key cost metric in FTQC - for constructing an $n$-variable data-lookup oracle. Additionally, exploiting ANF product terms allows for the exploration of space-time trade-offs, enabling the design of data-lookup oracles with distinct resource requirements that can adapt to varying system constraints - flexibility that current methods do not offer. Based on the target quantum system's requirements, our approach offers the ability to tailor oracle designs to minimize either Toffoli count and depth, or ancillary qubit usage.
272: Reacting flows are governed by the conservation equations of mass, momentum, energy, and chemical species, and exhibit strong nonlinearity due to convection and chemical reactions. As quantum computers are inherently limited to linear operations, a bridging method is required to enable their application to such nonlinear systems. This study proposes an approach using the Carleman linearization to integrate quantum computing into reacting flow analysis, with a focus on the nonlinear temperature dependence described by the Arrhenius equation. To handle the exponential form of the reaction rate, a Taylor series expansion is employed. The present method is validated through numerical simulations of fuel ignition. The impacts of the truncation order in the Carleman linearization and the polynomial order in the Taylor expansion are systematically examined. The results demonstrate that higher-order approximations enhance the accuracy but may also introduce numerical stiffness. Overall, the findings confirm the validity and potential of the proposed framework for quantum-assisted reacting flow computations.
273: Distributed quantum computation is a promising approach to building a fault-tolerant quantum computer at practical scale. To complete program execution within the minimum time, computational resources and communication resources should be assigned to reduce communication cost. Since remote lattice surgery operation between spatially separated quantum computers takes longer than local lattice surgery, minimizing delay due to the remote lattice surgery is a crucial issue to improve performance of distributed quantum computation. This delay is driven by three related issues: assignment of variable qubits to specific nodes; placement of those qubits within the nodes (resulting in contention for the limited number of local qubit movement paths); and contention for inter-node communication resources (both network interface communication qubits and channels) during concurrent operations. Focusing on the second problem, we propose placing qubits near the network interface based on their inter-node communication needs to avoid intra-node path collisions. We evaluate execution time of the VBE ripple-carry adder in a $2 \times 2$ grid topology, comparing our proposed qubit assignment approach to random placement. Our results suggest that the proposed model has the potential to reduce resource contention and to improve total execution time.
274: Qamomile is a software development kit specifically designed for quantum optimization. Unlike other quantum SDKs such as Qiskit or PennyLane, Qamomile provides a framework that bridges classical mathematical optimization models and quantum circuit representations by leveraging an intermediate representation. Acting as a bridge between classical problems and quantum computing, Qamomile provides broad compatibility and deployment flexibility. Qamomile supports a variety of quantum computing platforms including Qiskit, QURI Parts, PennyLane, QuTiP, QuEra, and CUDA-Q. By standardizing the workflow from problem definition to result analysis, Qamomile empowers researchers to perform consistent benchmarking and comparative studies across hardware and algorithmic strategies. This interface accelerates the exploration of quantum advantage in optimization tasks and enhances reproducibility in quantum algorithm research.
275: Trapped-ion quantum computers, leveraging a quantum charge-coupled device (QCCD) architecture, have world-class performance in the field of quantum computing, offering high fidelities and all-to-all connectivity [1]. While systems have advanced over the last decade, much work remains to scale quantum computers to fault-tolerance. Providing scalable light delivery is one key challenge. Current systems utilize engineered bulk- and fiber-optic-based light delivery systems, external to the vacuum chamber, to deliver arrays of beams to ions. However, fundamental optical limitations preclude the use of such systems when scaling beyond thousands of qubits. Integrated photonic-based beam delivery offers a potential solution, with encouraging proof-of-concept demonstrations from the photonics and quantum communities [2]–[5]. Quantinuum and Sandia National Labs have partnered to accelerate the development of integrated photonics for trapped-ion quantum computing applications, working towards photonic components supporting high-fidelity operations. Here, we present development of photonic integrated components designed to deliver laser light to $\text{Ba}^{+}$ qubits, utilizing a low-loss, high-confinement, trap-integrable PECVD SiN platform. In order to demonstrate two-qubit gates at 532 nm, we developed low loss, tight bend waveguides, efficient edge couplers, and asymmetric multimode interference (MMI) splitters, along with beam-forming grating out-couplers delivering gaussian beams at the ion plane. For quantum state preparation and measurement (SPAM) applications at $\text{4 9 3 ~ n m}$, we demonstrate fabrication-tolerant splitters and low-crosstalk gratings. Measured component performance shows promise for future trap-integrated demonstrations.
276: Quantum federated learning (QFL) is an emerging field that has the potential to revolutionize computation by taking advantage of quantum physics concepts in a distributed machine learning (ML) environment. However, the majority of available quantum simulators are primarily built for general quantum circuit simulation and do not include integrated support for machine learning tasks such as training, evaluation, and iterative optimization. Furthermore, designing and assessing quantum learning algorithms is still a difficult and resource-intensive task. Real-time updates are essential for observing model convergence, debugging quantum circuits, and making conscious choices during training with the use of limited resources. Furthermore, most current simulators fail to support the integration of user-specific data for training purposes, undermining the main purpose of using a simulator. In this study, we introduce SimQFL, a customized simulator that simplifies and accelerates QFL experiments in quantum network applications. SimQFL supports real-time, epoch-wise output development and visualization, allowing researchers to monitor the process of learning across each training round. Furthermore, SimQFL offers an intuitive and visually appealing interface that facilitates ease of use and seamless execution. Users can customize key variables such as the number of epochs, learning rates, number of clients, and quantum hyperparameters such as qubits and quantum layers, making the simulator suitable for various QFL applications. The system gives immediate feedback following each epoch by showing intermediate outcomes and dynamically illustrating learning curves. User can also upload their own data and check the simulation results using QFL without any fundamental knowledge. SimQFL is a practical and interactive platform enabling academics and developers to prototype, analyze, and tune quantum neural networks with greater transparency and control in distributed quantum networks.
277: Analog quantum simulations with Rydberg atoms in optical tweezers have emerged as a powerful tool for exploring strongly correlated many-body physics. However, the range of accessible phenomena remains limited by constraints in controlling many-body interactions in these systems. Here, we propose an alternative approach to realizing tunable interactions using Rydberg dressing on Aquila, a 256-atom quantum simulator based on optical tweezer arrays. By weakly admixing a Rydberg state via off-resonant laser coupling, we generate long-range interactions with temporal control. In combination with programmable atom geometries and site-selective control, this dressing protocol enables simulation of quantum spin models with state preparation and measurement in arbitrary basis. These capabilities enable access to exciting regimes of quantum simulation, including Quantum spin liquids, XYZ lattice models and broader application of quantum reservoir computing. Our approach establish Rydberg dressing as a practical and scalable tool for expanding the class of many-body systems accessible to analog quantum simulation and provides a critical stepping stone toward quantum machine learning and hybrid analog-digital quantum simulation with neutral atoms.
278: Simulating quantum circuits is essential for validating quantum algorithms. However, no single simulator consistently performs best - efficiency depends on circuit structure, entanglement, and depth. In this work, we integrate Qiskit-Aer (state-vector and matrix product state) and QTensor, a tree-tensor-network based simulator, into the Quantum Framework (QFw), a modular platform that supports multiple quantum backends via a unified interface. We also enable distributed quantum approximate optimization algorithm (DQAOA) application compatibility with QFw, allowing sub-problems to be solved in parallel at scale. We then benchmark DQAOA and TFIM (transverse field Ising model) circuits across supported simulators, showing how performance varies significantly with problem type. All simulations are deployed on the Frontier supercomputer using QFw's MPI-based orchestration for distributed, multinode execution. These results underscore the need for simulatoragnostic infrastructure to enable systematic evaluation and highperformance scaling of quantum workloads. QFw provides a practical and extensible path toward reproducible quantum algorithm development across diverse application domains.
279: We experimentally characterize a high-speed, low-loss switch and verify that entanglement is preserved when transmitting one photon of a polarization-entangled pair through all configurations of the switch. The preservation of entanglement through the switch demonstrates the utility of the switch for quantum networking applications.
280: This work presents QubiCML, a novel FPGA-based system engineered for real-time, in-situ discrimination of two- and three-level quantum states (quitrits) in superconducting quantum processors. Accurate and low-latency identification of quantum states is a critical enabler for scaling quantum computing, particularly as higher-dimensional systems such as qutrits are explored to increase information density, circuit depth, and gate expressivity. QubiCML integrates a lightweight, multi-layer neural network directly into FPGA hardware to classify the qutrit states $\vert g\rangle,\vert e\rangle$, and $\vert f\rangle$ with high fidelity and minimal latency. Traditional state discrimination methods rely on offline post-processing, resulting in delays incompatible with the short coherence times of superconducting qubits. QubiCML overcomes this bottleneck by performing all inference operations within the FPGA fabric itself, achieving full quantum state discrimination within 66 ns (with softmax) or 40 ns (without softmax). The system supports fast reconfiguration via BRAM-stored parameters, enabling compatibility with varying quantum hardware and dynamic calibration environments. Additionally, we propose FPGA-friendly techniques for data normalization and fixed-point quantization to eliminate the overhead of floating-point and division operations—further optimizing the architecture for real-time deployment. We evaluate QubiCML on in-house superconducting hardware across multiple qubits and qutrits. The system achieves up to 97 % average accuracy for qutrits and up to 99 % for two-level systems, using readout windows as short as 650-750 ns. These results establish QubiCML as one of the first practical implementations of real-time qutrit state discrimination, marking an essential step toward mid-circuit measurements, dynamic feedback, and advanced error correction in higher-dimensional quantum computing.
281: The improvement of quantum computing technologies relies on the reduction of flux noise that contributes to decoherence. Recent work has shown that the majority of flux noise is due to impurities and defects on the surface of the qubits [1], [2]. Electron spin resonance (ESR) is a prime candidate to detect these defects, but lacks the sensitivity and ability to provide information on the physical location of the defects. We report upon ESR measurements utilizing a non-resonant probe integrated within a semiconductor wafer probing station which could be used to detect paramagnetic defects believed to contribute to flux noise in quantum devices. Our approach greatly enhances ESR's sensitivity and provides a high spatial resolution on the surface of unaltered fully processed wafers and devices at room temperature. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method to detect defects on the surface of materials with a spin sensitivity improvement of roughly $10,000 × compared to classical ESR. The integration of a non-resonant probe into a standard semiconductor wafer probing setup has already been shown to be able to obtain a 2D map of unpaired spins on the surface of samples [3]. The technique offers a pathway for characterization of the defects which contribute to flux noise, which would provide critical insight into reducing decoherence mechanisms.
282: Neutral atom quantum computing's great scaling potential has resulted in it emerging as a popular modality in recent years. For state preparation, atoms are loaded stochastically and have to be detected and rearranged at runtime to create a predetermined initial configuration for circuit execution. Such rearrangement schemes either suffer from low parallelizability for acousto-optic deflector (AOD)-based approaches or are comparatively slow in case of spatial light modulators (SLMs). In our work, we introduce an algorithm that can improve the parallelizability of the former. Since the transfer of atoms from static SLM traps to AOD-generated movable traps is detrimental both in terms of atom loss rates and execution time, our approach is based on highly-parallel composite moves where many atoms are picked up simultaneously and maneuvered into target positions that may be comparatively distant. We see that our algorithm outperforms its alternatives for near-term devices with up to around 1000 qubits and has the potential to scale up to several thousand with further optimizations.
283: We explore how quantum computing (QC) can advance transportation optimization, with a focus on two high-impact areas: traffic signal control and vehicle electrification with grid integration. As transportation systems grow in complexity, classical optimization methods increasingly struggle to deliver scalable and efficient solutions, particularly for real-time environments. This work identifies key challenges within these two domains where QC may offer advantages, particularly in handling combinatorial decision spaces and dynamic constraints. We begin by outlining the limitations of classical approaches for traffic signal control optimization and electric vehicle charging coordination, highlighting where computational limitations arise. Previous quantum formulations are discussed to demonstrate how emerging quantum algorithms, including quantum annealing and hybrid algorithms, could be leveraged to reformulate and address these problems. We also evaluate the suitability of current quantum hardware and discuss the advantages that QC could bring to these domains. While acknowledging the present limitations of QC technologies, this poster emphasizes the importance of preparing quantum-compatible models today. By reviewing and establishing formulations that align with the strengths of quantum algorithms, researchers and practitioners can better position themselves to take advantage of QC advancements as they occur. This work aims to provide a practical, forward-looking perspective on the near-term potential of quantum computing in transportation optimization. Quantum Computing Transportation Optimization Traffic Signal Control Electric Vehicle Charging
284: Ising machines, quantum annealing (QA) machines, are promising for solving combinatorial optimization problems at high speed. Problems are formulated as Ising models where optimal solutions correspond to ground states, but stochastic noise often causes deviations, necessitating error reduction strategies. The quantum annealing correction (QAC) model introduces penalty spins to favor consistent solutions across replicas and has shown effectiveness in QA, but its behavior under simulated annealing (SA) remains insufficiently understood. This study systematically evaluates the stacked model, a recently proposed error reduction method, against QAC-based and simple parallelization approaches in SA. Our results demonstrate that, even for large-scale systems, the stacked model consistently outperforms alternatives as the number of replicas increases, maintaining relatively high success probability through spontaneous replica alignment via structured coupling. These findings highlight the stacked model as a scalable and error reduction framework for Ising-based optimization.
285: Implementing arbitrary-angle rotation gates is a fundamental task in Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing (FTQC). Over the past decade, researchers have focused on minimizing the $\mathbf{T}$-count in the Clifford+T decomposition based on the Solovay-Kitaev theorem. Recently, however, the advances in T-gate preparation techniques known as the zero-level distillation have significantly reduced the cost of $T$ gates, and the main research focus has been shifted to simpler and more efficient synthesis protocols. In this paper, we propose a method to prepare the magic state for arbitrary-angle $\mathbf{R Z}$ gates using the Linear Combination of Unitaries (LCU) framework, where the RZ gate is represented as a linear combination of $I$ and iZ with positive integer coefficients. The unique feature of our protocol is that for angles whose tangent is rational, our protocol can prepare the magic state with no approximation error. Using this property, our protocol is expected to improve the accuracy of high-precision quantum algorithms. Moreover, the number of Clifford+T gates is proportional to the number of ancilla qubits, which is the same order as the previous methods. We also address the issue of the probabilistic behavior of the magic state preparation and injection and show that these issues can be mitigated by parallelizing the preparation process and combining our protocol with other approximation methods.
286: We explore covert entanglement generation over the lossy thermal-noise bosonic channel, which is a quantummechanical model of many practical settings, including optical, microwave, and radio-frequency (RF) channels. Covert communication ensures that an adversary is unable to detect the presence of transmissions, which are concealed in channel noise. While covert communication of classical bits is well studied, covert quantum communication and entanglement generation remain largely unexplored. Here, we first show that a square root law (SRL) for covert classical secret communication over the lossy thermal-noise bosonic channel, defining the optimal rate and covert capacity $L_{\text{sec }}$. The achievable construction relies on position-based coding, sequential decoding, and quadrature phase-shift keying. Furthermore, we adapt the code used in covert secret communication to show that a square root law (SRL) for covert entanglement generation similar to that for classical: $L_{\text{EG}} \sqrt{n}$ entangled bits (ebits) can be generated covertly and reliably over $n$ uses of a bosonic channel. We report a single-letter expression for optimal $L_{\text{EG}}$ as well as an achievable method. We additionally analyze the performance of covert entanglement generation using single- and dual-rail photonic qubits for varying channel parameters. Despite a performance gap compared to the optimal strategy, these encodings may be more practical for physical implementation.
287: Quantum computing, while allowing for processing information exponentially faster than classical computing, is far from becoming a personal commodity. Indeed, because of cost and needs for ultra-cold temperature, shielded environment, and complex wiring for control, access to quantum computers is likely to be provided remotely, through quantum servers. Sharing quantum hardware between multiple users enables the efficient use of quantum resources, but makes some security threats possible. For instance, previous studies demonstrated that crosstalk between attacker and victim's qubits can be exploited to mount security attacks. In this work, we address the problem of securing user circuits submitted to quantum servers. We propose the Qubit Allocation for Inter-Circuit Crosstalk Countermeasure (QAICCC), which aims to maximize qubit usage, reduce inter-circuit crosstalk as well as intra-circuit noise. QAICCC performs (1) a crosstalk analysis of the targeted quantum processor to determine qubits involved in crosstalk with the largest intensity; (2) the allocation of qubits in the safest possible way; and (3) the application of existing techniques to further reduce crosstalk between circuits and noise in user circuits. The main contribution is the allocation algorithm, which aims to maximize qubit usage (including making unused qubits available for future usage) while minimizing the largest inter-circuit crosstalk error rate. Thus, QAICCC will support quantum computing adoption by securing the usage of quantum servers by a large number of actors.
288: Quantum simulation of the interactions of fermions and bosons - the fundamental particles of nature - is essential for modeling complex quantum systems in material science, chemistry and high-energy physics and has been proposed as a promising application of fermion-boson quantum computers, which overcome the overhead encountered in mapping fermions and bosons to qubits. However, compiling the simulation of specific fermion-boson Hamiltonians into the natively available fermion-boson gate set is challenging. In particular, the large local dimension of bosons renders matrix-based compilation methods, as used for qubits and in existing tools such as Bosonic Qiskit or OpenFermion, challenging. We overcome this issue by introducing a novel symbolic compiler based on matrix-free symbolic manipulation of second quantised Hamiltonians, which automates the decomposition of fermion-boson second quantized problems into qubit-boson instruction set architectures. This integration establishes a comprehensive pipeline for simulating quantum systems on emerging qubit-boson and fermion-boson hardware, paving the way for their large-scale usage.
289: Ising machines, including quantum annealers, have attracted much attention as an efficient solver for COPs (Combinatorial optimization problems). The SVR (Spin-Variable Reduction) method maps a COP with linear equality constraints to QUBO (Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization) model, which is a common input for using the Ising machines. In this paper, we conduct a tuning of a constraint coefficient for this method using Quadratic Assignment Problems as a case study. We find that the optimal value of the constraint coefficient can be either larger or smaller than that used in the conventional penalty method, depending on the problem instance. We discuss the underlying mechanism responsible for this difference.
290: Solving optimization problems is critical across many research domains, but the high dimensionality of parameter spaces often poses significant challenges. The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) has emerged as a promising approach for accelerating optimization in the Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) era by leveraging both classical and quantum computational resources. However, its performance can vary depending on the underlying quantum hardware architecture. In this work, we evaluate the performance of QAOA on different quantum hardware platforms, specifically, superconducting transmon qubits and trapped-ion qubits, targetting real-world optimization problems formulated as fully connected Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) instances. We evaluate both the solution quality and time-to-solution using dense QUBO matrices. Furthermore, we show that large-scale problems, such as a 100-bit QUBO instance, can be effectively tackled by integrating quantum computing with high-performance computing (HPC) resources. This study provides practical insights into the strengths and limitations of different qubit technologies and advances the application of quantum computing in solving real-world optimization problems.
291: The wire-cutting technique has been recently developed to partition a large quantum circuit into smaller subcircuits, enabling distributed computation across multiple quantum devices with limited capacity. In this work, we generalize the standard wire-cutting method—which can be interpreted as excising an identity operation—to a broader framework that allows the excision of arbitrary unitary gates. We propose a general measure-and-prepare approach to realize this extension, which allows a quantum gate to be excised from a circuit significantly more efficiently than by cutting all the wires surrounding the gate, leading to exponential savings in classical computational cost with respect to the number of wires involved. As an application, we employ this framework for the classical simulation of near-Clifford quantum circuits by excising non-Clifford gates from the circuit and efficiently simulating the remaining Clifford subcircuit in polynomial time. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of our method over the prior wire-cutting technique in emulating near-Clifford circuits.
292: In this work, the Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) algorithm has been used to train various Variational Quantum Circuits (VQCs). This approach is motivated by the fact that commonly used gradient-based optimization methods can suffer from the barren plateaus problem. PSO is a stochastic optimization technique inspired by the collective behavior of a swarm of birds. The dimension of the swarm, the number of iterations of the algorithm, and the number of trainable parameters can be set. In this study, PSO has been used to train the entire structure of VQCs, allowing it to select which quantum gates to apply, the target qubits, and the rotation angle, in case a rotation is chosen. The algorithm is restricted to choosing from four types of gates: Rx, Ry, Rz, and cNOT. The proposed optimization approach has been tested on various datasets of the MedMNIST, which is a collection of biomedical image datasets designed for image classification tasks. Performance has been compared with the results achieved by classical stochastic gradient descent applied to a predefined VQC. The results show that the PSO can achieve comparable or even better classification accuracy across multiple datasets, despite the PSO using a lower number of quantum gates than the VQC used with gradient descent optimization.
293: We propose and experimentally demonstrate a technique for achieving quantum control of spin qubits by utilizing localized magnetic fields generated by nanomagnets and skyrmions. The implementation of precise, localized control fields is critical to minimizing gate errors and cross-talk between neighboring qubits. In our theoretical work, we explored the use of nanomagnets and divergent and convergent magnetic skyrmions to generate a control field capable of manipulating spin qubits with high fidelity. Skyrmions, which resemble 3D hedgehog structures, offer advantages in standard semiconductor processes due to their 2D nature. Our simulations show that skyrmion configurations can provide gate fidelities above 99.9 % for singlequbit gates, while significantly reducing cross-talk in neighboring qubits compared to proximal nanomagnets. Expanding on this theoretical foundation, we experimentally demonstrate coherent quantum control of a nitrogen vacancy (NV) center in diamond using microwave fields from a nanoscale magnet, driven by a surface acoustic wave in lithium niobate. We observe highcontrast Rabi oscillations and control over the Rabi frequency by varying acoustic power. This approach, based on nanoscale magnets, provides a pathway to highly localized, energy-efficient quantum control and could replace thermally noisy microwave circuits, contributing to the scalability of quantum computing and sensing with NV defects and other spin qubits.
294: Qubit capacity is a common bottleneck in quantum computers, limiting the ability to run complex algorithms and slowing the advancements in quantum computing applications. Reusing qubits by resetting them after measuring and repurposing them for subsequent gate operations offers an effective strategy to reduce the overall qubit requirements. Based on Satisfiability Modulo Theories (SMT) and Integer Linear Programming (ILP), we present an optimal algorithm that maximizes qubit reuse while optionally constraining the circuit depth to a specified upper bound. Our approach considers all feasible circuit rearrangements to enhance optimality, including gate reordering and eager measurement. We further propose a divide-and-conquer approach to scale for large circuits by relaxing the optimality guarantee. Experimental results show that our exact method substantially decreases both the qubit count and the circuit depth compared to the current state of the art, while the divide-and-conquer approach effectively addresses scalability issues with maintained solution quality.
295: Quantum computation and error correction in higher dimensional systems offer a promising route to more efficient and robust codes and circuits, compared to qubits. In this work, we present a novel qutrit $[\![ 6,2,2 ]\!]_{3}$ quantum error correcting code with a transversal implementation of the binary AND gate. The key insight in our approach is that we can interpret a symmetric T-depth one circuit decomposition — composed of a CX circuit, $\mathrm{T}$ and $\mathrm{T}^{\dagger}$ gates, followed by the CX circuit in reverse — as a distance 1 CSS code. We thereafter increase the code distance by augmenting the code circuit with additional stabilizers while preserving the “built-in” transversal logical binary AND. As a result, we can leverage qutrit Clifford+T circuit synthesis to combine the advantages of quantum error correction and qudits, and moreover protect against leakage errors to higher levels.
296: Quantum machine learning is a promising direction for building more efficient and expressive models, particularly in domains where understanding complex, structured data is critical. We present the Quantum Graph Transformer (QGT), a hybrid graph-based architecture that integrates a quantum self-attention mechanism into the message-passing framework for structured language modeling. The attention mechanism is implemented using parameterized quantum circuits (PQCs), which enable the model to capture rich contextual relationships while significantly reducing the number of trainable parameters compared to classical attention mechanisms. We evaluate QGT on five sentiment classification benchmarks. Experimental results demonstrate that QGT effectively learns sentiment representations, achieving accuracies of 93.0%, 90.5%, and 88.0% on the Yelp, IMDB, and Amazon datasets, and 100% and 95.12% on the synthetic MC and RP datasets, respectively. These results highlight the potential of graph-based quantum NLP techniques for advancing efficient and scalable language understanding.
297: We present a novel algorithm that converts CTQWs on arbitrary graphs into efficient quantum circuits through graph matching decomposition. Our approach decomposes the target graph into a set of matchings, where a matching is a collection of disjoint edges that can be implemented exactly using multi-controlled rotation gates. The overall CTQW evolution is then approximated via Trotterization over these matchings. We validate our approach through comprehensive comparison with Pauli decomposition methods across all connected isomorphic 8-vertex graphs, demonstrating comparable accuracy across all test cases. Our matching decomposition achieves reduced gate counts compared to Pauli decomposition for approximately 33% of all connected 8-vertex graphs, with particular advantages for graphs that decompose into small numbers of matchings or contain many disjoint edges. Our matching decomposition provides a valuable alternative pathway for implementing CTQW-based algorithms on near-term gate-based quantum devices while maintaining the fundamental quantum advantages of walk-based computation.
298: Quantum circuit synthesis is fundamental to the advancement and realization of quantum computing. To support both researchers and learners in exploring the structure and behavior of quantum circuits, this paper presents a dedicated interactive visualization platform specifically designed for quantum circuit synthesis: the Quantum Circuit Synthesis Visualizer (QSynViz). The platform offers intuitive circuit editing, matrix visualization, target-to-circuit distance computation, and dynamic tracking of the synthesis process. By making circuit structures and optimization trajectories visually accessible, QSynViz enables users to directly observe, analyze, and refine circuit designs. Bridging visual intuition with algorithmic insight, QSynViz serves as a powerful tool for circuit optimization, synthesis algorithm evaluation, and quantum computing education.
299: Quantum and quantum-inspired optimization (QIO) offer strong potential for solving complex optimization problems. This paper is the first to apply QIO in a real-world industrial setting, where it is used to efficiently optimize the hyperparameters of an AI-driven Aluminum Extrusion Profile Temperature Prediction Model, based on eXtreme Gradient Boosting (AEPTPM-X). AEPTPM-X aims to enable isothermal extrusion by accurately predicting profile temperatures in real time, thereby enhancing product quality and reducing waste. Experimental results show that QIO significantly improves prediction accuracy, indicating a promising direction for intelligent manufacturing and fostering broader adoption of QIO in real-world applications.
300: Simulation of fermionic systems is one of the most promising applications of quantum computers. It spans problems in quantum chemistry, high-energy physics and condensed matter. Underpinning the core steps of any quantum simulation algorithm, fermion-qubit mappings translate the fermionic interactions to the operators and states of quantum computers. This translation is highly non-trivial: a burgeoning supply of fermion-qubit mappings has arisen over the past twenty years to address the limited resources of early quantum technology. Previous literature has presented a dichotomy between ancillafree fermion-qubit mappings, which minimise qubit count, and local encodings, which minimise gate complexity. We present two computational approaches to the construction of general mappings while working with a limited number of qubits, striking a balance between the low-qubit and low-gate demands of present quantum technology. The first method frames the order of fermionic labels as an instance of the quadratic assignment problem to minimize the total and maximum Pauli weights in a problem Hamiltonian. We compare the orderoptimized performance of several common ancilla-free mappings on systems of size up to 225 fermionic modes. The second method is a computational approach to incrementally add ancilla qubits to Jordan-Wigner transformations and further reduce the Pauli weights. By adding up to 10 ancilla qubits, we were able to reduce the total Pauli weight by as much as 67 % in JordanWigner transformations of fermionic systems with up to 64 modes, outperforming the previous state-of-the-art ancilla-free mappings. Reproducibility: source code and data are available at https://github.com/cameton/QCE_QubitAssignment
301: We present a quantum cognitive model that can be implemented on a quantum machine. This model uses solutions of the Schrödinger equation to model human cognitive control and decision making in a standard paradigm in psychology: the two-alternative forced-choice (2AFC) task, where participants are forced to choose between two competing alternatives. In the model, the two alternatives map to a multiple square well potential energy function. The depths of the wells correspond to attentional control, while the widths corresponds to features of the stimulus. Using this potential energy, the time-independent Schrodinger equation can be solved for an energy eigenstate basis of the bound states of the system, with higher energies corresponding to higher levels of focus. The full time-dependent Hamiltonian involves an oscillating field that evolves the system from ground state to superpositions of the excited states. The probabilities of the choices in the task are calculated as the probability of finding particles in a particular potential well. Furthermore, the quantum framing of this problem makes this problem suitable for mapping to quantum computing implementations. The state of the system follows the trajectory of a ground state, which can be mapped to a variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) implementation. Meanwhile, the time-dependency and oscillating field can be simulated using current quantum simulation methods and Rabi oscillations. Since our problems can be mapped onto currently-available NISQ prototypes of 2040 qubits, they represent an application domain with tractable near-term quantum-computing resource requirements.
302: Quantum computers are growing at a rapid pace. Trends show that the current decade could be the one in which quantum computers deliver commercial value. Today's quantum computers are overwhelmed by errors. To unlock their massive potential, a significant reduction in errors is required. Several qubit technologies are under research, e.g. superconducting, neutral atoms, trapped ions, photons and silicon. For useful quantum computing on these qubit technologies, Quantum Error Correction (QEC) turns unreliable physical qubits into useful logical qubits. QEC requires solving a real-time, large data volume decoding problem that determines the effect of physical noise on the computation carried out on logical qubits. The nature of the decoding problem depends on the qubit technology, choice of QEC code and mode of quantum computation. These are actively researched subjects in the quantum computing world. Hardware-based decoders that use Field Programmable Gate Array (FPGA) or Application Specific Integrated Circuits (ASIC) technologies are the most promising solutions in terms of speed and scalability. However, the design methodology for these solutions typically suffers from long lead times and a lack of flexibility. We propose GridGenQ, a hardware design utility that automates part of the FPGA/ASIC design methodology for distributed QEC decoders. We show that with our novel solution, development time for such distributed hardware decoders can be reduced from several weeks to few minutes. This allows for fast prototyping of distributed decoder architectures to meet the requirements posed by a dynamic QEC landscape.
303: In this study, we report that quantum quasi-cyclic low-density parity-check codes decoded via joint belief propagation exhibit steep error-rate curves, despite the presence of error floors. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first observation of such threshold-like behavior for quantum codes with non-vanishing coding rate, excluding those decoded with non-binary BP decoders. Moreover, we find that dominant error events contributing to the error floor typically involve only a small number of bits. These findings suggest that the error floor is caused by trapping sets—specific subgraph structures in the Tanner graph—and indicate that identifying and avoiding such structures may lead to further reduction of the error floor.
304: Optimizing the topology of plasmonic nanoparticles to achieve desired optical properties is a computationally intensive task due to the high cost of electromagnetic simulations. We present a framework that leverages active learning with a surrogate Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) model to accelerate this process. We compared the performance of three optimization heuristics: Classical Genetic Algorithm (CGA), Quantum-Inspired Genetic Algorithm (QIGA), and hybrid Quantum-Assisted Genetic Algorithm (QAGA) that uses Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) for targeted mutations. We tested these methods on $5 \times 5$ and $10 \times 10$ grid optimization problems for gold (Au) nanoparticles. Our initial findings for the $5 \times 5$ problem show that the QIGA achieves the highest fitness of 0.266. For the more complex 10×10 problem, the QAGA demonstrates superior performance, achieving the highest fitness of 0.291. Our results highlight the promise of quantum and quantum-inspired techniques while also revealing the significant challenges in scaling these hybrid algorithms.
305: Effective fertilizer allocation enhances agricultural productivity and sustainability. Traditional heuristics often cause nutrient imbalance and excess cost. This study introduces a quantum-inspired Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) model solved by the Compal GPU Annealer (CGA). Experiments on radish, cabbage, and rice demonstrated 8-20% cost savings over greedy heuristics. A small-scale Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) validation using IBM Qiskit confirmed quantum algorithmic compatibility.
306: Crosstalk remains a major obstacle to building scalable and fault-tolerant quantum computers. Conventional diagnostic techniques-often based on numerical simulation or statistical modeling-struggle to scale with hardware complexity and offer limited interpretability. In this work, we present a visual analytics framework for diagnosing qubit crosstalk using lightweight, circuit-based models integrated with an interactive user interface. Our approach quantifies correlations between active and idle qubits under parameterized single- and twoqubit operations, enabling detection of both spatial and gateinduced crosstalk. The system incorporates qubit topology and gate performance data to support sector-based exploration and correlation mapping. This tool assists users in identifying correlated error sources, informing qubit placement strategies, and guiding noise-aware circuit design.
307: Recent advances in quantum architectures and computing have motivated the development of new optimizing compilers for quantum programs or circuits. Even though steady progress has been made, existing quantum optimization techniques remain asymptotically and practically inefficient. Because many global quantum circuit optimization problems belong to the complexity class QMA (the quantum analog of NP) [51], it is not clear whether efficiency guarantees can be achieved. In this paper, we present an algorithm that achieves efficiency by aiming at a form of local optimality rather than global optimality. Our local-optimization algorithm cuts a circuit into subcircuits, optimizes each subcircuit with the specified oracle optimizer, and melds the subcircuits by optimizing across the cuts lazily as needed. To prove efficiency, we show that, under some assumptions, the main optimization phase of the algorithm requires a linear number of calls to the oracle optimizer. Our empirical results show that our local-optimization algorithm can outperform existing optimizers significantly, by more than an order of magnitude on average. Perhaps surprisingly, the algorithm achieves these improvements without noticeable degradation in optimization quality. These results show that local optimization can be effective for optimizing quantum circuits.
308: This poster proposes an on-chip optical pulse modulation system for scalable superconducting quantum computers. Towards the scalable design, qubit control systems need to be located in the cryogenic environment to reduce the number of interconnections across the room temperature and the cryogenic regions. The cryogenic CMOS-based qubit control system is a promising approach, yet it is a bottleneck that exhausts the cooling capacity of the dilution refrigerator. In order to eliminate this bottleneck while providing the ability to control multiple quibits with a minimum necessary number of interconnections, this poster extends the RoF (Radio-over-Fiber) system where optical signals are directly fed from the Room Temperature (RT) region to a PD (PhotoDetector) mounted near the transmon qubit through low-loss and high-speed fibers. Unlike the conventional RoF system, the proposed system employs cryogenic silicon photonics-based modulators in the intermediate part for executing gate operations individually at each transmon qubit with a minimum necessary number of fibers across the RT and the cryogenic regions. Evaluation results show that the proposed system eliminates the power consumption by 79.5% compared with the cryogenic CMOS-based design. The proposed system achieves comparable gate fidelity to the control system generating fully customized RF pulses in the RT environment.
309: In this paper, we explore the performance of the quantum-inspired Quantum Extreme Learning Machine (QELM) for molecular property prediction using regression.
